notes.meaning: God's people respond to His rescue with personal thanksgiving. Although the Lord showed righteous anger toward their sin, He has now set that anger aside and brought gentle comfort. Believers can rest peacefully knowing that God's mercy has taken the place of judgment.

differ.view: Some dispensational teachers hold that this song will be sung literally by the surviving remnant of Israel when Christ reigns on earth during the millennium.
Reformed Christians understand this song as belonging to the church throughout the entire reign of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Earlier critical scholars often viewed this chapter as a separate, later hymn attached to the book rather than written by Isaiah himself.

notes.meaning: Salvation comes from the power of the Lord alone, never from human effort. God Himself becomes the shield, strength, and joy of His people, repeating the victory song Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea. Trusting completely in God removes fear from the heart.

God's rescue is described as an endless, bubbling spring of water in a dry land. The Jewish people later remembered this promise during the Feast of Tabernacles by carrying water from the Pool of Siloam with great joy. In the same way, believers gladly receive the life-giving grace of God that never runs dry.

differ.view: Many Baptists highlight Christ as the spring, with faith as the God-given bucket used to receive His grace through prayer and Scripture.
Some Lutherans connect drawing this saving, life-giving water to the gift of baptism.

notes.meaning: The joy of being saved cannot remain hidden inside one person. Believers call on each other to praise the Lord and tell all nations about what He has done. Sharing God's great works helps spread the knowledge of His glory to people everywhere.

Worshippers are invited to sing out loud because the Lord has performed wonderful deeds of deliverance. His victory over sin and death is far too great to keep secret. God's people are called to set an active example of praise so that the whole earth learns of His goodness.

The citizens of Zion, representing God's gathered people, are told to shout for joy. Their greatest blessing is not earthly wealth or safety, but the living presence of the Holy One of Israel dwelling in their midst. Having the holy and great God near gives His church lasting hope and happiness.
